content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate almond milk is a beverage made from ground almonds, water and cocoa mass. It combines a mild nutty flavor with the sweet‑bitter notes of chocolate and is often used as a plant‑based alternative to dairy milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almond milk originated in the Mediterranean as a way to use surplus nuts.
The chocolate version became popular in the 1990s with the rise of plant‑based diets.
Cocoa mass used in the drink is rich in flavonoids that may support heart health.
Almond milk contains fewer calories than cow’s milk while retaining some healthy fats and vitamins.
In some countries the drink is sold as a concentrate that is diluted with water before consumption.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almond milk provides a good amount of vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: Although lower in protein than dairy milk, it supplies amino acids useful for vegetarians.

items.title: Low sugar (when unsweetened)
items.content: Unsweetened versions contain minimal sugar, making them suitable for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: The cocoa component adds flavonoids that may improve vascular function.

items.title: Lactose‑ and gluten‑free
items.content: The product is safe for people with lactose intolerance and gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Almond milk can trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to nuts.

items.title: Added sugar in sweetened versions
items.content: Chocolate drinks are often sweetened, increasing calories and affecting blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low calcium content
items.content: Regular almond milk contains little calcium unless it is fortified.

items.title: Additives and preservatives
items.content: Some commercial products contain emulsifiers or stabilizers that may not suit everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink chocolate almond milk chilled, add it to smoothies, oatmeal, coffee, or use it in baking as a dairy substitute. For a richer taste, gently warm the beverage with a pinch of cinnamon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the opened container in the refrigerator and consume within 5‑7 days. Seal tightly to prevent absorption of other odors. Frozen almond milk can be stored for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings, deep‑fried and coated in a hot sauce, are a staple of fast‑food menus and casual restaurants. They are juicy, crispy on the outside, and deliver a bold, spicy flavor thanks to a sauce made from chili peppers, vinegar, and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are commonly served in portions of 6 to 12 pieces.
Hot sauce heat can range from mildly spicy to extreme levels of heat.
In the United States, wings gained popularity in bars during the 1970s.
There are many sauce variations: Buffalo, habanero, curry‑chili, and more.
Wings are often accompanied by celery sticks and blue‑cheese dressing to balance the heat.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Wings contain niacin, B6, and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from chicken helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Capsaicin in hot sauce
items.content: Capsaicin may boost metabolism and has mild analgesic properties.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The sauce often contains a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Hot sauce can irritate the stomach lining in people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken protein.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Fried wings and sauce add a significant amount of calories.

items.title: Trans fats from improper frying
items.content: Reusing oil can lead to the formation of trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wings are typically eaten by hand, pulling the meat off the bone. Serve them with blue‑cheese dressing, celery, carrot sticks, or potato wedges. To tame the heat, offer a cooling dip such as ranch or yogurt‑based sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked wings in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven or microwave, avoiding repeated frying.

content.title: About
content.content: Steamed flounder retains most of its nutrients, offering a delicate flavor and tender texture. Steaming requires no added fat, keeping the fish low‑calorie and high in protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flounder belongs to the flatfish family and is commonly farmed in freshwater ponds.
Steaming preserves omega‑3 fatty acids, which are beneficial for heart health.
Wild flounder can grow up to 1.5 kg, but commercial portions are usually smaller.
Traditional preparations include grilling or baking, but steaming yields a milder taste.
Flounder is a good source of B‑vitamins, especially B12, important for the nervous system.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Contains EPA and DHA, which support cardiovascular health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption and supports immune function.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and potassium
items.content: Selenium protects cells from oxidative stress, while potassium helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Steamed flounder has roughly 120 kcal per 100 g, making it a diet‑friendly option.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Wild-caught flounder can accumulate mercury and other toxins; choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt or sauces can increase sodium levels, which is a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steamed flounder can be served as a main dish, added to salads, rice, or vegetable sides. It pairs well with lemon, dill, olive oil, and light yogurt‑based sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep flounder in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in vacuum‑sealed packaging and use within 3 months.

oatmeal-instant-plain-made-with-non-dair.title: Instant plain oatmeal made with non‑dairy milk, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Instant oatmeal is made from whole oat groats that are steamed and dried so they dissolve quickly in hot water or plant‑based milk. The dairy‑free version is suitable for vegetarians and people with lactose intolerance. Added plant fat (e.g., coconut or sunflower oil) raises the energy content and gives a creamier texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats have been cultivated for more than 5,000 years and are one of the oldest grain crops.
Instant flakes are produced from whole oat kernels, not from refined bran, preserving most nutrients.
Adding plant fat increases the calorie count to about 200‑250 kcal per serving.
Oats contain beta‑glucan, a soluble fiber that helps lower cholesterol.
In many countries oatmeal is commonly served with berries, nuts, or honey.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan supports heart health, lowers LDL cholesterol, and enhances immune function.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Provides a slow‑release energy that keeps you feeling full longer.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation and immune response.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Supplies thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats.

items.title: High calorie content with added fat
items.content: A serving with added plant fat can contain up to 250 kcal, so portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Phytic acid presence
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or heat treatment lowers its level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour 200 ml of hot water or plant‑based milk over the oats, stir, and let stand for 1‑2 minutes. Optionally top with fresh berries, dried fruit, nuts, or honey. It can also be microwaved: 1 minute on high, then stir.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal tightly or transfer to an airtight container. Shelf life is typically 12 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn chips with sweet flavors are crunchy snacks made from whole corn kernels that are toasted to a golden hue and coated with a sweet glaze. They combine the lightness of popcorn with the crisp texture of chips, and a variety of flavors (strawberry, caramel, vanilla) make them a popular choice for a sweet bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn chips first appeared in the United States in the early 2000s as an alternative to traditional potato chips.
The sweet glaze is often made from sugar, honey, or maple syrup, giving the product a characteristic caramel aroma.
Unlike regular popcorn, the chips undergo an additional pressing step, making them denser and crunchier.
There are more than 10 sweet flavor variants, including berry, fruit and dessert combinations.
Popcorn chips are frequently used as decorative toppings for desserts and cocktails.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with most potato chips, popcorn chips usually contain less saturated fat, especially when baked rather than deep‑fried.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Corn is rich in dietary fiber, which supports normal digestive function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Sweet flavors are often enriched with berry extracts that provide vitamin C and polyphenols.

items.title: Quick source of glucose
items.content: The sugar in the glaze raises blood glucose rapidly, which can be useful for quick energy replenishment.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Corn chips are typically gluten‑free, making them suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The sweet glaze makes the product calorie‑dense and may contribute to tooth decay with frequent consumption.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to corn, experiencing skin or digestive reactions.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Some varieties may contain artificial flavors, colors, and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite low fat, the sugar and starch make the snack fairly caloric; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popcorn chips are convenient as a stand‑alone snack, tossed into ice cream, yogurt, or used as a topping for desserts. They can also be mixed with nuts and dried fruit for a more filling trail mix.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn chips in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. When stored properly they retain their crunch and flavor for up to 3 months. Discard any chips that develop off‑flavors or a stale smell.

content.title: About
content.content: Porcupine balls are tender pieces of porcupine meat, pan‑seared to a golden crust and served with a fragrant mushroom sauce. The dish balances the mildly sweet flavor of the meat with the earthy notes of mushrooms, creating a harmonious blend of texture and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Porcupine is considered a delicacy in regions where the animal is traditionally hunted.
The mushroom sauce is typically made from button mushrooms, cream, and herbs such as thyme and parsley.
The balls are often accompanied by mashed potatoes or fresh vegetable sides.
The dish is popular in restaurants that specialize in exotic cuisine.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Porcupine meat provides a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many red meats, porcupine contains relatively low levels of saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meal supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from mushrooms
items.content: Mushroom sauce delivers selenium and polysaccharides that have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Allergy to exotic meat
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to wild‑game meat.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Porcupine meat is rich in purines, which can be problematic for people with gout.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Improper cooking may lead to food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the balls hot, drizzled with mushroom sauce. Pair them with boiled potatoes, rice, or a fresh vegetable salad. For extra richness, stir a knob of butter into the sauce before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked balls in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Store the mushroom sauce separately for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly to a rolling boil to ensure safety.

rice-brown-with-peas-no-added-fat.title: Brown Rice with Peas, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with peas, no added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of whole grain brown rice and green peas. It contains no added oils, salt, or sugar, making it a convenient healthy‑meal option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, providing more fiber and nutrients than white rice.
Peas are a good source of plant protein and vitamin C.
The rice‑pea combination offers a near‑complete amino‑acid profile.
This product is commonly used in school cafeterias and athlete nutrition programs.
The lack of added fat makes calorie counting easy.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Brown rice provides soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Peas add about 5 g of protein per 100 g of product, beneficial for vegetarians and active individuals.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The rice supplies B1, B3, and B6 vitamins essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Contains magnesium, phosphorus, and iron, supporting muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: No added fat makes it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Pea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Glycemic impact
items.content: While lower than white rice, brown rice can still raise blood glucose if eaten in large portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready after heating in the microwave or on the stovetop. It can be served as a side dish, added to salads, or eaten on its own as a quick meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a sealed container. After opening, use within 3–4 days or keep refrigerated.

content.title: About
content.content: Sloe gin fizz is a classic cocktail made with gin, sloe berries, lemon juice and sparkling water. It is refreshing, lightly sweet‑tart, with a distinctive berry‑forward aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink first appeared in the early 1920s in the United Kingdom.
Sloe berries are macerated in gin for several weeks to create sloe gin.
It is traditionally served in a highball glass over ice.
Fresh lemon juice is used in the original recipe, though lime is sometimes substituted.
The cocktail is popular in summer because of its light carbonation.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: When consumed in moderation, the cocktail contains fewer calories than many sweet mixed drinks.

items.title: Vitamin C from lemon
items.content: Lemon juice provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Antioxidants from sloe berries
items.content: Sloe berries are rich in anthocyanins, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: The drink contains alcohol and should be consumed responsibly; avoid during pregnancy, driving, or by children.

items.title: Gin allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to gin or to sloe berries.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lemon juice increases acidity and may irritate the stomach of people with gastritis.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: Combine 45 ml sloe gin, 15 ml fresh lemon juice and 10 ml simple syrup in a shaker with ice. Shake well, strain into a highball glass over fresh ice and top with sparkling water. Garnish with a lemon wedge or a sloe berry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Sloe gin should be stored in a cool, dark place, tightly sealed, for up to 2 years. Sloe berries keep best in the refrigerator in an airtight container, and the finished cocktail should be enjoyed immediately to retain its fizz.
